title: The Sharpe Pint: AI Capex Panic, the Hamada Equation, and Why Trend-Following Broke

opening_mood.text: Alright? Grab a coffee—or something stronger if you've been staring at the after-hours tech screens. Q2 earnings season is officially in 'spill-your-drink' territory, with Alphabet and Tesla showing that the AI arms race is incredibly real, but also eye-wateringly expensive. Meanwhile, the FTSE had a rare day in the sun thanks to cooling inflation, and we've got a brilliant line-up today covering everything from stripping beta to its birthday suit to why high-frequency traders killed a 200-year-old trend strategy. Let's get into it.

content.text: Q2 earnings season is in full swing, and the big tech giants are laying bare the brutal reality of the AI arms race. Meanwhile, central banks are navigating geopolitical minefields, and global capital flows are on the verge of a massive structural shake-up.
1. Alphabet's AI Cloud Soars, but the Capex Bill Spooks the Street

Alphabet reported its Q2 2026 earnings, posting a massive 24% YoY revenue growth to $119.8 billion and an EPS of $9.11, absolutely smashing Wall Street forecasts of $2.88. The star of the show was Google Cloud, which accelerated by an eye-watering 82% to $24.8 billion, driven by enterprise AI infrastructure and Gemini adoption. However, the stock dipped after hours as investors focused on the massive capital expenditure required to keep this AI engine running.

Why it matters: This proves that AI monetisation is actually happening—this isn't just a paper boom. But it also highlights the brutal reality of the AI arms race: you have to spend tens of billions on chips and data centres just to stay in the game.

The City angle: For asset managers and equity analysts, the debate is shifting from 'Is AI real?' to 'What is the return on invested capital (ROIC) of this capex?' Tech concentration remains a massive risk if margins start to compress under the weight of these infrastructure bills.
2. Tesla's Margin Squeeze: Record Deliveries, Massive Profit Miss

Tesla's Q2 2026 results were a classic split. Revenue beat expectations at $28.24 billion (up 26% YoY) on record deliveries of 480,216 vehicles. But adjusted EPS missed badly, coming in at $0.33 vs. $0.53 expected, as margins were squeezed and capex surged 142% YoY to $5.8 billion. Elon Musk defended the spend, pointing to aggressive investments in AI, Optimus, and Robotaxis. Shares fell roughly 4% after hours.

Why it matters: Tesla is trying to transition from a car company to an AI and robotics powerhouse, but that transition is incredibly capital-intensive. Squeezed auto margins and negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion are testing investors' patience.

The City angle: This is a classic valuation conundrum. If you value Tesla as an auto OEM, it looks wildly overvalued. If you value it as an AI/robotics play, you have to swallow massive execution risk and cash burn.
3. ECB Pauses to Assess Middle East War Risks, but September Hike Looms

The European Central Bank is widely expected to hold its key deposit rate steady at 2.25% today, pausing after its June hike. The pause is intended to give policymakers time to assess the economic fallout of the renewed conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed Brent crude back up toward $95 a barrel.

Why it matters: While Eurozone inflation has cooled slightly, the geopolitical energy shock is keeping central bankers on high alert. Swap markets are already pricing in an 85-90% probability of a 25 bps rate hike in September.

The City angle: Fixed income and macro desks will be parsing Christine Lagarde's press conference for any hawkish tilts. If she signals that the ECB is ready to hike again to combat energy-driven inflation, expect European bond yields to creep up.
4. Japan Urges the World's Largest Pension Fund to Bring Capital Home

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and her cabinet are pushing a major economic strategy to transition Japan into a 'growth-oriented economy.' Crucially, Takaichi urged the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF)—the world's largest pension fund with %1293.6 trillion ($1.81 trillion) in assets—to increase its investments in domestic financial assets. The yen rallied on expectations of a massive capital repatriation.

Why it matters: For decades, Japanese institutional capital has flooded global markets in search of yield. If the GPIF starts repatriating even a fraction of its portfolio back into Japanese equities and bonds (especially now that Japan has positive interest rates), it will reshape global capital flows.

The City angle: This is a massive thematic play for global macro and asset allocation. A stronger yen and rising Japanese bond yields could put upward pressure on global yields as Japanese investors buy fewer US Treasuries and European bonds.
5. Geely and Ford's Spanish Plant Deal: Dodging Tariffs via Factory Sharing

Chinese automotive giant Geely has struck a landmark deal to buy/share part of Ford's underused Almussafes factory near Valencia, Spain. Geely will use the idle assembly line to manufacture its compact EX2 electric vehicle inside the EU, effectively sidestepping the hefty tariffs slapped on Chinese EV imports.

Why it matters: This is a brilliant piece of regulatory arbitrage. Instead of fighting EU tariffs, Chinese EV makers are simply buying up underutilised European factory capacity. For Ford, it cuts fixed costs and protects local jobs at a plant running at less than a quarter of its 450,000-vehicle capacity.

The City angle: This highlights the restructuring pressure facing legacy European automakers and the speed at which Chinese OEMs are adapting. Expect more cross-border joint ventures and asset sales as European legacy players look to monetise their idle capacity.
6. British Business Bank Backs Odyssey Ventures to Stop the UK AI Brain Drain

The state-owned British Business Bank (BBB) committed %110 million to Odyssey Ventures, a transatlantic VC firm, alongside its $50 million early-stage fund, Odyssey Discovery I. The fund focuses on UK founders building at the intersection of AI and Deeptech, acting as a 'transatlantic bridge' to help them scale globally with US capital and customers from day one.

Why it matters: The UK is world-class at spawning AI and deeptech startups, but historically, they've been starved of scale-up capital compared to their US peers, leading to a massive 'brain drain' or premature acquisitions.

The City angle: For venture capital and private equity, this highlights the growing role of state-backed cornerstone capital in anchoring early-stage funds. It also shows that the transatlantic corridor remains the primary route for scaling European deeptech.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: The AI Capex Hangover

content.text: If you want to understand the current mood in the City, look no further than the 'Mag 7 Split' that played out after the New York bell last night. Alphabet and Tesla both dropped their Q2 numbers, and the message from the market was loud and clear: we believe in your AI dream, but we’re starting to sweat over the electricity bill.

First, the numbers. On Wednesday, the S&P 500 slipped 0.14% to close at 7,498.96, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.56% to 25,690.90. But the real action was in the after-hours sandbox. Alphabet delivered a blowout revenue figure of $119.8 billion (up 24% YoY), powered by an absolute monster of a quarter for Google Cloud, which surged 82% to $24.8 billion. On pure product demand, Google is flying. But then CFO Anat Ashkenazi walked the full-year capex guidance up to a staggering $195B–$205B. The market choked on its coffee, sending the stock down 3% after hours. The growth is real, but the cash burn is getting scary.

Tesla offered a much grimmer version of the same story. While revenue beat at $28.24 billion, adjusted EPS came in at a measly $0.33 (missing the $0.51 consensus by a mile), free cash flow went negative by $1.1 billion, and operating margins collapsed. Elon is spending like a drunken sailor on AI, robotaxis, and robotics—capex surged 142% YoY to $5.8 billion—while having to heavily discount his actual cars to move them. The stock slid 4% after hours. It’s a classic split: the AI arms race is showing up in the top line, but it’s eating the bottom line alive.

Meanwhile, back in London, the FTSE 100 had a rare moment in the sun on Wednesday, rallying 1.2% to close at 10,716.97—its highest level since March. The catalyst? A beautiful downside surprise in UK inflation. June CPI cooled to 2.6% (down from 2.8% in May), giving the Bank of England plenty of breathing room and sparking a broad risk-on rally in domestic equities, banks, and housebuilders. Even the looming %114bn takeover of FTSE 100 warehouse giant Segro by US rival Prologis couldn't dampen the mood, though it’s another depressing reminder of UK Plc being bought on the cheap.

But don't get too comfortable. The macro backdrop is getting increasingly messy. Brent crude has surged past $96 a barrel (touching $98 on Thursday morning) as the US-Iran conflict escalates, with Houthis striking Red Sea tankers and the US launching its 12th consecutive night of strikes. This geopolitical flare-up is pushing US 10-year Treasury yields back up to a two-month high of 4.67%, reminding everyone that inflation risks are far from dead. It’s also weighing on European markets this morning, with the STOXX 600 down 0.5%—not helped by chipmaker STMicroelectronics plunging 15% on a weak Q3 outlook.

What’s the cross-asset read here? Underneath the surface, markets are telling us that the 'easy' phase of the AI trade is over. Multiples are stretched, and investors are no longer willing to hand over blank cheques for 'future potential' if it means negative free cash flow today. At the same time, the bond market is flashing warning signs that geopolitical energy shocks could keep central banks hawkish for longer. If you're in an interview or chatting at the pub today, the talking point is simple: we are transitioning from an 'AI hype' market to an 'AI ROI' market, and the margin for error has just got a whole lot thinner.

sections.title: Financial Idea: Stripping Beta to its Birthday Suit

content.text: The Hamada Equation: Stripping Beta to its Birthday Suit

If you’ve ever sat through a corporate finance class or prepped for an investment banking interview, you’ve probably memorised the steps to unlever and lever beta. But outside of the textbook, why do we actually do this? And why does it matter to anyone managing real money?

At its core, a stock's beta measures its systematic risk relative to the market. But that risk is actually made of two entirely different things: business risk (how volatile are the underlying cash flows?) and financial risk (how much debt is piled on top?). If you look at a company's raw public beta, you are looking at a messy combination of both. To compare companies fairly—or to value a private business—you need to strip away the financial noise. Enter the Hamada Equation.
The Mechanics: How to Unlever and Lever

To find the pure, unadulterated business risk (the 'unlevered beta' or 'asset beta'), we strip out the debt. First published by University of Chicago professor Robert Hamada in 1972, the formula combines the Modigliani-Miller theorem with the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM). The standard formula is:
Beta_Unlevered = Beta_Levered / [1 + (1 - Tax Rate) * (Debt / Equity)]

Once you have the unlevered beta, you can compare it across peers. For example, a highly levered utility company and a cash-rich utility company might have very different levered betas, but their unlevered betas (the risk of actually generating electricity) should be very similar.
If you are valuing a private target or modeling an LBO, you then 're-lever' this asset beta using the target's proposed capital structure:
Beta_Levered = Beta_Unlevered * [1 + (1 - Tax Rate) * (Debt / Equity)]
A Quick Walkthrough
Imagine you’re looking at 'PubCo', a debt-free chain of London pubs with a beta of 1.0. Because it has zero debt, its levered beta is exactly equal to its unlevered beta (1.0).

Now, a private equity sponsor wants to buy PubCo in an LBO. They plan to fund the acquisition with a 60/40 debt-to-equity ratio (meaning Debt/Equity = 1.5). Assuming a corporate tax rate of 25%, what happens to the beta of the equity?
Using the Hamada Equation:

By loading the company with debt, the equity beta has more than doubled from 1.0 to 2.125. Under CAPM, this means the cost of equity will skyrocket. The business itself isn't selling any more or less beer, but the equity holders are now taking on massive financial risk, and they demand to be paid for it.
Why This Matters in the Real World

items: LBO Valuation: In a leveraged buyout, you cannot use the target's historical cost of equity to discount cash flows. The massive debt load increases the equity risk. You must unlever the peer betas, find the industry average asset risk, and then re-lever it at the LBO's high debt levels to get an accurate cost of equity.

Capital Structure Optimisation: Corporates use this to find their optimal capital structure. If they issue debt to buy back shares, their levered beta rises, which increases the cost of equity. They have to balance the benefit of the tax shield against the rising cost of equity.

Asset Management: When comparing companies, looking at levered beta can be deceptive. A company might look 'low risk' (low beta) simply because it has a massive cash pile (negative net debt). Unlevering the beta reveals the true riskiness of the underlying operations.

content.text: The Classic Interview Trap
In an interview, you will almost certainly get asked this trick question: 'If a company issues debt to buy back shares, what happens to its unlevered beta? And what happens to its levered beta?'

The rookie mistake is to say both increase. The correct answer is: The unlevered beta stays exactly the same. Unlevered beta represents the fundamental risk of the business operations, which haven't changed (they are still selling the same products). The levered beta, however, will increase because the company now has more debt relative to equity, raising the financial risk for equity holders.
How to use this in conversation
Next time someone points to a tech giant's low beta as proof of its 'defensive business model', you can sound like the smartest person in the room by saying:

"Sure, their public beta is low, but they are sitting on $50 billion of net cash. If you actually unlever that beta to look at the pure asset risk, and then re-lever it to a normal capital structure, you'd see the underlying business is far more cyclical than the stock price suggests."

sections.title: Quant & AI: Tail-GAN & The Art of Not Underestimating a Market Crash

content.text: The Idea: Tail-GAN & The Art of Not Underestimating a Market Crash

If you have ever tried to train a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to simulate financial market paths, you have probably run into a frustrating truth: standard GANs are 'tail-blind'. Because extreme market crashes (the 1% or 2.5% worst days) are rare, a standard discriminator focuses almost entirely on matching the bulk of the distribution—the 98% of normal, boring days. If your generator gets the tail completely wrong, the discriminator barely penalises it. For risk managers trying to simulate stress-testing scenarios or calculate capital requirements under Basel III's Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), this tail-blindness is a fast track to getting fired.

This is where Tail-GAN steps in. Proposed by Rama Cont, Mihai Cucuringu, Renyuan Xu, and Chao Zhang (published in Management Science), Tail-GAN forces the generator to respect the extreme edges of the distribution. The secret sauce? A beautiful concept from statistical decision theory called joint elicitability.
The Mechanics: The Fissler-Ziegel (FZ) Loss

A risk measure is 'elicitable' if you can define it as the unique minimizer of the expectation of some loss function. Value-at-Risk (VaR) is elicitable (using the pinball loss). But Expected Shortfall (ES)—the average loss given that you have breached your VaR—is famously not elicitable on its own. You cannot write a single loss function where the true ES is the unique mathematical minimum. However, in 2016, mathematicians Tobias Fissler and Johanna Ziegel proved that the pair (VaR, ES) is jointly elicitable using a family of joint loss functions known as the FZ loss.

Tail-GAN exploits this by replacing the standard GAN discriminator loss with the FZ0 loss function (a specific, scale-invariant version of the FZ loss). By evaluating the generated scenarios against the real data using this joint loss, the discriminator forces the generator to produce paths that perfectly match the historical VaR and ES of the assets.
A PyTorch Implementation of FZ0 Loss

Here is how you can implement the FZ0 loss function in PyTorch to train a tail-aware generator. Note that in this standard formulation, returns are negative in the tail (i.e., we are looking at losses, so Expected Shortfall and VaR are negative numbers).

import torch

def fz0_loss(y, v, e, alpha=0.05):
    """
    Computes the Fissler-Ziegel (FZ0) loss for joint VaR and ES.
    Assumes returns y, VaR v, and ES e are negative (left-tail returns).
    
    y: Tensor of actual returns (shape: [batch_size])
    v: Tensor of predicted VaR (shape: [batch_size])
    e: Tensor of predicted ES (shape: [batch_size])
    alpha: Quantile level (e.g., 0.05)
    """
    # Ensure ES is strictly negative to avoid division by zero or log issues
    e = torch.clamp(e, max=-1e-5)
    
    # Indicator function: 1 if return is worse than (less than) VaR
    indicator = (y <= v).float()
    
    # FZ0 loss formula
    term1 = - (1.0 / (alpha * e)) * indicator * (v - y)
    term2 = v / e
    term3 = torch.log(-e)
    
    loss = term1 + term2 + term3 - 1.0
    return torch.mean(loss)
Why This Matters for Your Next Interview or Coffee Chat

items: The Pub/Interview Question: "How do you generate realistic stress-testing scenarios for a multi-asset portfolio?"

The Smart Answer: "Standard generative models like WGANs are tail-blind because they optimize for global Wasserstein distance, which ignores rare events. To fix this, you can use Tail-GAN, which incorporates the Fissler-Ziegel (FZ0) joint loss function. This exploits the joint elicitability of VaR and Expected Shortfall to force the generator to match the actual tail risk of the historical distribution, even across dynamic trading strategies."

Why it lands: It shows you aren't just copy-pasting generic AI hype. You understand the mathematical limitations of GANs, the nuances of risk measures (VaR vs. ES), and the regulatory reality of FRTB.

content.text: The Catch (Caveats & Risks)

items: Non-Differentiability: The indicator function in the FZ0 loss is non-differentiable. To actually train this in PyTorch, you have to swap the step function for a smooth approximation (like a sigmoid with a low temperature parameter) so that gradients can flow back to the generator.

Sign Sensitivity: The FZ0 formulation assumes that returns are negative in the tail. If your data is scaled differently, or if you are modeling positive losses directly, you have to flip the signs carefully, or the log(-e) term will break your code.

sections.title: The Paper: The Plumbing That Killed a 200-Year-Old Strategy

content.text: The Plumbing That Killed a 200-Year-Old Strategy

If you have spent any time looking at CTA (Commodity Trading Advisor) performance over the last decade, you will know that short-term trend-following has been a bit of a dog. For nearly two centuries, buying what was going up and selling what was going down was the closest thing to a financial cheat code. Then, around 2009, the fast-trend machine simply broke. Sharpe ratios for short-horizon trend strategies collapsed from a healthy 1.5 down to basically zero. The standard industry excuse has always been "crowding"—too many quants chasing the same signals. But a brilliant paper from the team at Capital Fund Management (CFM), led by quant legend Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, finally offers a convincing "why". It is not capacity, it is not electronification, and it is not that the market suddenly became perfectly efficient. It is the plumbing.
The Paper
Title: "Is Trend Still Your Friend? A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following"
Authors: Jutta G. Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and Jean-Philippe Bouchaud (Capital Fund Management / Imperial College London)
Source: arXiv:2607.01550 (July 2026)
The Core Idea: The Self-Fulfilling Loop

To understand why trend died, you first have to understand why it ever worked in the first place. Bouchaud and his co-authors argue that trend-following is not just a passive risk premium. It is a self-fulfilling feedback loop. First, a fast moving average crossover triggers a buy signal. Second, trend followers place aggressive market orders to buy. Third, the market impact of these buy orders pushes the price up. Finally, this price rise reinforces the trend signal, triggering the next batch of trend followers to buy. In other words, trend followers do not just harvest momentum; their own trading activity actually creates and sustains it. But this loop relies on one crucial assumption: that trend followers can execute their trades aggressively at a reasonable cost.
Enter the HFTs and the Tick-Size Split

Post-2008, the market-making landscape changed forever. The old-school, inventory-tolerant bank desks were replaced by high-frequency trading (HFT) firms. HFTs are incredibly sharp, but they hate holding risk and they absolutely despise being run over by predictable, directional flow (like a CTA buying over several hours). The authors show that the single variable separating dead trends from surviving ones is the volatility-normalised tick size. This creates a stark dichotomy in how HFTs behave:

items: Small-Tick Contracts (e.g., FX, Equity Index Futures): Here, the tick size is tiny relative to daily volatility. The limit order book is "sparse" (thin). When HFTs detect a predictable trend-following order, they immediately withdraw their liquidity or jump ahead of the queue. Because the book is thin, the price instantly gaps against the CTA. The execution cost eats the entire PnL, and the self-fulfilling loop is severed.

Large-Tick Contracts (e.g., Bonds, Short-Term Interest Rates, some Commodities): Here, the tick size is large relative to volatility. The order book is "dense" with massive queues at each price level. HFTs cannot easily jump the queue or withdraw liquidity without losing their spot. The depth remains robust, the execution costs remain low, and the self-fulfilling loop continues to function.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: Trend is active, not passive: Momentum is a product of market impact, not just behavioural biases or macro trends.
Microstructure beats macro: A macro-level anomaly that worked for 200 years was permanently broken by a microscopic change in how liquidity is provided.

Faster is not better: If you are running fast trend signals on small-tick contracts, you are essentially donating your alpha to HFT market makers. The edge is not just expensive to trade—it is structurally gone.

content.text: What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skim the heavy econophysics math in the middle of the paper where they model limit order book dynamics and prove the feedback loop stability. Instead, focus on the empirical charts in Section 3. The divergence in cumulative PnL between small-tick and large-tick contracts post-2008 is one of the cleanest, most striking charts you will see in empirical finance.
The Pub/Coffee Talk
Next time you are having a pint with a colleague or sitting in an interview, here is how to sound like the smartest person in the room:

"We always talk about 'crowding' as the reason quant strategies decay, but the CFM paper shows it is actually a microstructural story. Fast trend-following on FX and equities was killed because HFT market makers withdraw liquidity the moment they spot predictable CTA flow. Because those are small-tick markets, the price gaps instantly and severs the feedback loop that created the trend in the first place. If you want trend to work today, you have to trade large-tick contracts where HFTs cannot easily pull their quotes."
Our Take

This paper is a masterclass in why understanding market microstructure matters, even for macro or long-term investors. It proves that markets are not passive, frictionless pools where prices magically reflect fundamental value. They are complex, adaptive systems where the plumbing dictates the price action. When the plumbing changes, the anomalies vanish. It is also a healthy reminder that backtests spanning 200 years are useless if the underlying market-making regime has shifted.

content.text: The Compromise Effect (Extremeness Aversion)

Ever stood at a pub bar, looked at the wine list, and ordered the second-cheapest bottle? Of course you have. You don't want to look like a cheapskate by ordering the house plonk, but you also don't want to blow sixty quid on a Barolo you can't appreciate. That instinct—to steer clear of the extremes and settle for the safe, cosy middle—is a powerful psychological quirk known as the Compromise Effect, or extremeness aversion.

First formalised by Stanford professor Itamar Simonson in his seminal 1989 paper, 'Choice Based on Reasons', the Compromise Effect proves that our preferences aren't absolute; they are highly contextual. Simonson showed that if you offer people a choice between a cheap, basic camera and a pricey, advanced one, the split is fairly even. But if you introduce a third, ultra-premium, eye-wateringly expensive camera, something magic happens: the previously 'overpriced' advanced camera suddenly becomes the highly popular, 'sensible middle' choice.

Why does this happen? Because our brains hate having to justify extreme decisions to others (or to ourselves). Choosing the middle option minimises the risk of regret. It feels like the most rational, easily defensible compromise. 'I didn't buy the cheap rubbish, but I didn't waste money on the gold-plated version either.'

In the City, this is your secret weapon for pricing, pitching, and fee negotiations. If you present a client with a binary choice—say, a standard advisory fee of 1.2% versus a premium service at 1.8%—they will likely negotiate you down to the bone. But if you introduce a third 'Platinum Bespoke' tier at 2.5% (which includes a load of high-touch, labour-intensive fluff you don't actually want to do), the 1.8% tier suddenly looks like the bargain of the century. They feel like they've made a prudent, balanced decision, and you get the exact fee you wanted.

The same applies to asset management. If you show a client just two portfolios—one low-risk/low-yield and one high-risk/high-yield—they often freeze, paralysed by the fear of making the wrong extreme choice. Introduce a 'Balanced' middle portfolio, and they will flock to it. It's not because they've done a deep mathematical optimisation of their utility function; it's because the middle option feels safe.

How you can use it: Next time you are pitching a proposal, a fee structure, or an investment strategy, never present a binary choice. Always offer three tiers. Design the third, most expensive tier to be slightly absurd—just enough to make your actual target (the middle tier) look like the only sensible, value-packed compromise.
To sell the sensible middle, you must first build the gold-plated extreme.
